title: Retinoblastoma
subject: Pathology
summary: A malignant retinal tumour in children, usually unilateral, caused by loss of the Rb tumour suppressor. It presents with leukocoria and can metastasise if untreated.

sections.p: Retinoblastoma is a primary intraocular malignancy of the retina, most common in children under five. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging and, if possible, cytogenetics.

t.b: Detects intraocular mass, calcifications, and extraocular extension. A mass with speckled echoes suggests retinoblastoma.
Assesses extraocular spread and optic nerve invasion. A tumour extending beyond the globe is a red flag.
Documents tumour location and size; useful for monitoring.
Identifies hereditary cases; informs family counselling.

sections.p: The International Intraocular Retinoblastoma Classification (IIRC) stages A–E based on tumour size, location, and extraocular spread.
b: A: Small tumour <5mm, no subretinal fluid
C: Tumour >10mm or optic nerve invasion

sections.p: The classic two‑hit hypothesis: one germline RB1 mutation (familial) and one somatic hit (sporadic).

t.b: Can predispose to aggressive tumour behaviour due to immunosuppression.
May delay presentation and worsen prognosis.

sections.p: Children present with a white pupil, sometimes with eye misalignment. Vision loss may be subtle early on.
Use bedside and imaging tests that are available locally; if advanced imaging is unavailable, rely on clinical exam and ultrasound.

t.b: Detects tumour and calcification; absence of calcification may suggest other lesions.
Baseline for chemotherapy; abnormal values may delay treatment.

sections.p: Extraocular spread, optic nerve invasion, and metastasis to bone or liver are life‑threatening.
Multidisciplinary approach: local therapy for small tumours, systemic chemotherapy for advanced disease, and surgery if needed.
b: External beam radiotherapy – avoided in children due to secondary malignancy risk
Enucleation – definitive for advanced intraocular disease

t.b: First‑line systemic agent; chosen for efficacy and lower neurotoxicity compared to others.
Added in multi‑agent regimens; monitor renal function.
Used when resistance develops; watch for myelosuppression.

sections.p: Regular ophthalmic exams, genetic counselling for families, and early detection programmes reduce morbidity.
b: Screening at birth in high‑risk families
Education on early signs for parents

sections.p: Other causes of leukocoria should be ruled out.
b: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous – fibrovascular stalk

sections.p: Calcifications may be absent in early tumours; normal B‑scan does not exclude small lesions.
b: Early tumour may show no calcification
Low‑resolution ultrasound may miss small masses

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid eye pain or vision loss
Sudden onset of leukocoria in a child
Signs of systemic spread (fever, weight loss)

faq.q: What is the most common presentation of retinoblastoma?
faq.a: Leukocoria, often noticed by parents when the child looks at a bright light.
When the tumour is large, involves the optic nerve, or has spread beyond the eye, removal prevents metastasis.
Yes, about 30% are familial due to germline RB1 mutations; these children need genetic counselling.

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with a white pupil. What is the first investigation? — B‑scan ultrasonography to detect tumour and calcification.
You suspect retinoblastoma but the B‑scan is normal. What next? — Consider MRI or repeat exam; early tumours may lack calcification.
A child with retinoblastoma is scheduled for chemotherapy. Which drug is avoided in children and why? — Radiotherapy is avoided due to risk of secondary malignancy.
You find optic nerve invasion on MRI. What is the management? — Enucleation to prevent extraocular spread.
A sibling of a child with retinoblastoma is 2 years old. What screening is recommended? — Annual ophthalmic examination and genetic counselling.
You observe leukocoria in a 6‑month‑old. What differential should be considered? — Coats disease, persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous, congenital cataract.
